slides.heading: Three Ways to Build a Sentence
bullets: Every sentence is built from one or more propositions (subject + predicate statements).
A Simple sentence has just one proposition.
A Compound sentence joins two or more complete sentences together.
A Complex sentence tucks a clause inside another.

slides.text: A Simple Sentence consists of a single proposition.
examples: one subject, one predicate — one complete thought

slides.text: A Compound Sentence is two or more complete sentences joined together, each making sense alone.
examples: Wheat grows in the field, and men reap it.
The wind blew, but the ship was safe.
Study hard, or you will fail.
each complete part is called a Member

slides.heading: Practice — Simple or Compound?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each sentence is simple or compound.
items: Rain fell, but we stayed dry.

slides.text: A Complex Sentence is one in which some element is a clause — a group with its own subject and predicate.
examples: I know where gold is found.
The book that I read was long.
one main statement, with a clause built into it

slides.heading: Principal & Subordinate Clauses
bullets: A complex sentence has a principal clause and at least one subordinate clause.
A Principal Clause makes complete sense by itself:  “I know…”
A Subordinate Clause does not make complete sense alone:  “…where gold is found.”
The subordinate clause does the work of a single element inside the sentence.

slides.heading: Practice — Principal or Subordinate?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each clause is principal (makes sense alone) or subordinate (does not).

slides.heading: Practice — Simple, Compound, or Complex?
slides.instruction: Name the kind of each sentence.
items: I know that you are here.
The book that I read was long.

slides.text: An Interjection is a word thrown into a sentence to express sudden feeling or emotion.
examples: it neither affirms nor denies — it just exclaims

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Interjection
slides.instruction: Name the interjection in each sentence.

slides.heading: The Eight Parts of Speech
bullets: Noun — names.   ·   Pronoun — stands in for a noun.
Verb — asserts action, being, or state.   ·   Adjective — describes or defines.
Adverb — modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb.   ·   Preposition — shows relation.
Every word you meet is doing one of these eight jobs — that is all of Part I.

items: What are the members of a compound sentence?
Name the eight parts of speech.
answers: One that consists of a single proposition.
Two or more complete sentences joined together.
The complete sentences it is made of.
One in which some element is a clause.
A clause that does not make complete sense alone.
A word that expresses sudden feeling or emotion.
Noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.
